stories.headline: War on drugs: J&K ranks 1st in PIT-NDPS detentions, 3rd in property attachments
stories.title: War on drugs: J&K ranks 1st in PIT-NDPS detentions, 3rd in property attachments
stories.summary: Jammu and Kashmir has emerged as one of the leading regions in the country in enforcement against the drug trade, ranking first in detentions under the Prevention of Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (PIT-NDPS) Act and third in property attachments. According to official figures presented as part of the administration’s drug de-addiction measures during a recent meeting convened by members of the NITI Aayog, 3,072 cases under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act have been registered in Jammu and Kashmir since January 1, 2026. The cases have resulted in 3,556 arrests and 376 convictions. The authorities have also attached 421 properties valued at Rs 196 crore and detained 169 persons under the PIT-NDPS Act. As part of regulatory and enforcement action against the drug network, 160 drug hotspots have been identified, while 1,698 suspects are currently under surveillance, the official figures show. Authorities have also cancelled 22 drug-store licences and suspended 400 licences as part of measures to prevent the diversion and misuse of controlled substances. The government has simultaneously intensified its crackdown on the illicit cultivation of narcotic crops. During the period, 12 acres of poppy and 144 acres of cannabis cultivation were destroyed. A total of 247 cases were registered in connection with such cultivation, leading to the arrest of 254 persons. The official data states that illegal poppy cultivation has been “nearly eliminated”. The enforcement drive has also extended to transport-related documents. Authorities have suspended 781 vehicle registrations and 669 driving licences in connection with drug-related cases. The administration has issued a common Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) governing the cancellation or suspension of documents and facilities of persons accused under the NDPS Act and those detained under the PIT-NDPS Act. The SOP covers passports, driving licences, arms licences, contractor licences, government accommodation and security. According to the framework, the objective is to restrict the mobility of accused persons, prevent misuse of identity and disrupt drug networks. “Trigger events for initiating action include an FIR involving commercial quantity, detention orders, court orders, intelligence inputs and conviction,” the official document states. Under the procedure, the investigating officer is required to prepare a case dossier containing the accused person’s identity details, relevant documents and particulars of the offence. A Look Out Circular (LOC) is then issued to prevent foreign travel. The SOP provides for cancellation or suspension of documents and facilities, including passports, driving licences, arms licences, security and government accommodation. Post-conviction measures are to ensure continuation of the cancellation or suspension and the LOC, as applicable. In cases of acquittal, the framework provides for restoration of documents and rights, withdrawal of the LOC and unfreezing of accounts. The SOP also calls for coordinated monitoring through clearly defined roles, timelines, nodal officers and mechanisms for reporting and review. Alongside enforcement, the government has reported a substantial expansion of treatment and counselling services for people affected by substance abuse. Since January 2026, treatment has been provided to 5,321 new out-patient department (OPD) cases and 801 new in-patient department (IPD) cases. The facilities have also recorded 1.79 lakh follow-up visits. The official figures show that 799 patients were discharged, while 15,054 patients received counselling. The government has also said that awareness campaigns were conducted across all panchayats through rallies, seminars and workshops.

stories.headline: India–Canada Reset: Building a Partnership for a Fragmented World
stories.title: India–Canada Reset: Building a Partnership for a Fragmented World
stories.summary: The world is entering an era in which old certainties are disappearing faster than new arrangements are taking shape. The post-Cold War belief in an increasingly integrated global economy has given way to geopolitical competition, strategic protectionism, fractured supply chains and a renewed contest for technology, energy and critical minerals. Europe remains unsettled by war; West Asia continues to experience profound instability; the United States and China are locked in an increasingly consequential strategic and economic competition; and countries across the Global South are demanding a greater voice in the institutions that govern the international system. It is against this unsettled backdrop that the emerging India–Canada rapprochement deserves to be viewed. What is taking place between New Delhi and Ottawa is more than a diplomatic thaw. It has the potential to become an important example of how two democracies can move beyond a period of profound disagreement and construct a relationship based on economic complementarity, strategic autonomy and institutional dialogue. The timing could not be more consequential. The inaugural India–Canada Finance Ministers’ Economic and Financial Dialogue held in Toronto on August 27 has given the reset a concrete economic foundation. The two countries have set an aspiration to expand bilateral trade to CAD 70 billion by 2030, while India has expressed readiness to begin negotiations on a Bilateral Investment Treaty. Cooperation is also being explored in financial technology, modern payment systems, cross-border remittances, capital markets and critical minerals. (Canada ) This is no longer diplomacy conducted primarily through statements. It is diplomacy being translated into institutions. From confrontation to strategic pragmatism India–Canada relations suffered a severe setback following Canadian allegations concerning the killing of Hardeep Singh Nijjar in British Columbia. The resulting diplomatic confrontation damaged political trust and disrupted normal high-level engagement. The lesson from that difficult period should not be that India and Canada have incompatible interests. The opposite is true. Their interests are sufficiently complementary that prolonged estrangement carries a cost for both. A mature bilateral relationship does not require two countries to agree on every question. Democracies will inevitably have differences over law, security, foreign policy and domestic politics. What matters is whether those differences are managed through evidence, due process, diplomacy and institutional channels. Canada has a responsibility to uphold its constitutional commitments, the rule of law and freedom of expression. India has an equally legitimate responsibility to protect its national security, territorial integrity and citizens from terrorism and violent extremism. These principles need not be contradictory. The present reset represents an important recognition on both sides that disagreements should be contained within the relationship rather than allowed to define it. That is the essence of mature diplomacy. Canada is looking beyond dependence Canada’s strategic circumstances have changed dramatically. For generations, the United States was the overwhelmingly dominant economic and strategic partner of Canada. Geographic proximity made this inevitable and economically advantageous. But the recent intensification of US–Canada trade tensions has demonstrated the vulnerability inherent in excessive dependence on a single market. Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has therefore placed greater emphasis on economic diversification and building new international partnerships. Canada’s present circumstances make that strategy not merely desirable but necessary. The breakdown of recent US–Canada trade negotiations and escalating tariff tensions have added urgency to Ottawa’s diversification strategy. (Reuters ) India naturally assumes significance in this search for diversification. India is not simply a large consumer market. It is a major economic, technological and geopolitical power with a young population, expanding infrastructure, growing energy requirements and an increasingly important role in the Indo-Pacific and the Global South. Canada, meanwhile, possesses precisely those resources and capabilities that India increasingly needs: energy, critical minerals, agricultural commodities, advanced technology, capital, research capacity and access to North American markets. The relationship therefore offers a rare combination of complementarity and scale. India’s economic rise meets Canada’s resource strength The next chapter in India–Canada relations should be built around economics. The recent Finance Ministers’ Dialogue demonstrates how rapidly the agenda is expanding. The two countries are looking at financial-sector cooperation, FinTech, capital markets, payment modernisation, cross-border remittances and merchant payments. Canada and India have also discussed expanding the use of India’s Unified Payments Interface in Canada. (Canada ) This is significant because modern diplomacy increasingly operates through economic infrastructure. A successful India–Canada economic relationship should encompass at least six strategic pillars. First, trade and investment. The proposed Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement should provide predictable rules for businesses and investors and create a framework extending well beyond traditional merchandise trade. Second, critical minerals. Canada’s resource base and India’s manufacturing ambitions create an obvious strategic partnership. Batteries, semiconductors, electric vehicles, renewable energy systems and advanced technologies all depend upon secure mineral supply chains. Third, energy security. India’s enormous and growing energy requirements create opportunities for Canadian LNG, clean energy, nuclear cooperation and other energy technologies. Fourth, technology and artificial intelligence. Both countries possess strong technology ecosystems and substantial pools of highly educated talent. Collaboration in AI, cybersecurity, quantum technologies and digital infrastructure could produce benefits well beyond the bilateral relationship. Fifth, financial cooperation. Canadian pension funds and institutional investors already have substantial exposure to India. Canada has acknowledged the significance of its long-term institutional capital in India’s development, while both sides are examining ways to deepen engagement between financial institutions and investors. (Canada ) Sixth, education and human capital. Universities, research institutions and professional networks can provide the intellectual infrastructure for the partnership. A CEPA concluded without these broader dimensions would be an opportunity missed. The Finance Ministers’ Dialogue: diplomacy becoming architecture The August 2026 Finance Ministers’ Dialogue deserves particular attention because it represents a shift from episodic diplomacy towards institutionalised economic engagement. The dialogue was established following the commitment made by Prime Minister Modi and Prime Minister Carney during their March 2026 meeting. Both governments have committed themselves to concluding CEPA negotiations by the end of 2026. (Canada ) This institutionalisation matters. Relationships become resilient when they are supported by permanent mechanisms rather than dependent upon individual leaders or temporary political moods. The India–Canada relationship now needs precisely such institutional resilience. Regular finance, trade, defence, science, technology, consular and migration dialogues should become permanent features of the relationship. The two Prime Ministers’ June meeting at the G7 Summit already reflected this broader approach. They welcomed progress on economic cooperation, resilient supply chains, energy security and CEPA, while also agreeing to launch negotiations on a General Security of Information Agreement and deepen defence and security cooperation. (PM of Canada ) That is a far more comprehensive relationship than the one that existed only a few years ago. The human bridge must become a strategic asset Perhaps the most extraordinary strength of India–Canada relations is the people-to-people connection. The Indian-origin community has become deeply embedded in Canadian economic, academic, cultural and political life. At the same time, Canada has developed generations of students, researchers, entrepreneurs and professionals with strong connections to India. This human bridge must be treated as an asset rather than a source of political contestation. Diaspora communities should never become instruments of geopolitical rivalry. Canada’s commitment to multiculturalism and freedom of expression deserves respect. But freedom of expression cannot become a shield for incitement to violence or terrorism. Conversely, allegations of foreign interference or transnational repression must be investigated through credible evidence and due process rather than political rhetoric. The objective should be to create a relationship in which the Indian diaspora feels secure in Canada, and Canada feels confident that its institutions are respected by India. That is entirely achievable. Security cannot be separated from friendship No serious analysis of India–Canada relations can avoid the security question. India has consistently expressed concern about extremist and separatist activities emanating from Canadian soil. Canada has raised concerns regarding foreign interference and transnational repression. These concerns require dialogue, not denial. The two countries should establish a sustained senior-level security mechanism involving diplomatic, intelligence and law-enforcement agencies. Cooperation should focus on terrorism, organised crime, money laundering, extortion, cybercrime and violent extremism. The Kanishka tragedy remains a terrible reminder of what happens when terrorism transcends national boundaries. The principle should be universal: terrorism and political violence cannot be legitimised by ideology, ethnicity, religion or political grievance. India and Canada can disagree profoundly on many political matters and still cooperate against violence. Indeed, that is what mature democracies should do. Two middle powers, one changing world The deeper significance of this rapprochement lies in the character of the two countries. India and Canada are not superpowers. Neither seeks to dominate the international system. Both, however, possess substantial economic, diplomatic, technological and human capital. This makes them important middle powers. The emerging international system will increasingly depend upon such countries. India has pursued strategic autonomy, maintaining relationships with the United States, Russia, Europe, Japan, the Gulf, Africa and the Global South. Canada is now attempting to diversify its external relationships while retaining its traditional partnerships. Their approaches are different, but their strategic requirement is increasingly similar: neither country wants its national interests to be determined entirely by the preferences of a larger power. This is where their partnership acquires a larger geopolitical meaning. India and Canada can help build a world of multiple partnerships rather than rigid blocs. The Indo-Pacific opportunity The Indo-Pacific provides another important area for convergence. India occupies a central strategic position in the Indian Ocean and is an essential actor in the Indo-Pacific. Canada, with its Pacific geography and expanding interest in the region, can become a constructive partner. Cooperation in maritime security, critical-mineral supply chains, infrastructure, clean energy, technology and freedom of navigation can strengthen the broader regional architecture. India has also supported Canada’s engagement with the Indian Ocean Rim Association, reflecting a growing recognition of the importance of Canadian participation in the wider Indo-Pacific framework. (PM of Canada ) The relationship should therefore not be confined to bilateral geography. It can become part of a larger Indo-Pacific strategy. From reset to strategic partnership The danger now is complacency. Diplomatic reconciliation can be fragile if it is not converted into institutional habits. India and Canada should therefore pursue a structured five-year roadmap. They should conclude CEPA with ambition and balance; begin serious investment-treaty negotiations; establish permanent financial and security dialogues; expand cooperation in critical minerals and energy; strengthen university and research partnerships; and create mechanisms for regular consultation between parliamentarians, businesses, civil society and diaspora representatives. The objective should be to ensure that no future bilateral disagreement can once again bring the entire relationship to a halt. The true test of diplomacy is not whether countries remain friendly when they agree. It is whether they remain engaged when they disagree. A partnership suited to the twenty-first century The India–Canada relationship should not be described merely as a return to normalcy. The old normal itself has disappeared. The international system today is more fragmented, more competitive and more uncertain. Economic security has become national security. Supply chains have become strategic assets. Technology has become a component of geopolitical power. Critical minerals have become as important to future economies as oil was to the industrial age. In such a world, countries need trusted partners across regions. India needs Canada for resources, capital, technology, education and access to North American markets. Canada needs India for economic diversification, a vast and growing market, technology partnerships, investment opportunities and a stronger connection with the Indo-Pacific. But both need something even more important: dependable democratic partnerships in an uncertain international environment. That is why the present India–Canada reset should be seen as an opportunity of historic proportions. The task before New Delhi and Ottawa is not to forget their disagreements. It is to develop the political maturity to prevent those disagreements from destroying the larger relationship. The future should move from estrangement to engagement, from episodic diplomacy to institutional partnership, from suspicion to evidence-based cooperation, and from limited commerce to comprehensive economic interdependence. If that transformation succeeds, India and Canada will have achieved something larger than a bilateral reconciliation. They will have demonstrated that democracies can disagree without becoming adversaries; that strategic autonomy does not mean strategic isolation; and that economic interdependence can coexist with national sovereignty. In a fragmented world, that lesson matters. The future international order will not be built only by the great powers. It will also be shaped by countries willing to create bridges across geopolitical divides. India and Canada have an opportunity to become such bridge-builders. Their relationship can be a model of what twenty-first-century diplomacy should look like: principled but pragmatic, sovereign but interconnected, commercially ambitious but strategically responsible, and capable of turning disagreement into dialogue rather than estrangement. The reset has begun. The real challenge now is to give it permanence, purpose and strategic depth. In a world increasingly divided into competing camps, India and Canada should choose partnership—not because they agree on everything, but because they understand that their shared interests are greater than their differences. (The author is a political analyst, a constitutional thinker and a senior advocate in the Supreme Court of India)

stories.summary: TECHNOLOGY & NATIONAL SECURITY In 1999, during the Kargil conflict, India asked the United States for GPS data over the heights and was turned down. That refusal is the founding document of India's own satellite navigation programme. NavIC exists because somebody in Washington decided Indian soldiers did not need to know where they were standing. Twenty-seven years on, the government has made Indian time legally binding. Four weeks earlier, the same government had told Parliament that NavIC could no longer fix a position on its own. A mandate arrives before the machinery Rule 7 is the widest clause. No entity may use, display or record any time reference other than IST, for any purpose. Storing timestamps in Coordinated Universal Time is ordinary practice in server logs worldwide. MediaNama, which reported the rules first, has asked the department and has no answer yet. Rule 6(4) then makes accuracy the responsibility of whoever uses the signal rather than whoever supplies it, and Rule 6(5) requires that user to monitor deviation, log it, and prove traceability to the national standard. A stock exchange does this already. A cooperative bank or a regional internet provider in Srinagar does not. The rules take effect 180 days after gazette publication, placing commencement in early 2027. The constellation that cannot navigate On 29 July, in a written reply in the Lok Sabha, Minister of State for Space Dr Jitendra Singh told the House that only three NavIC satellites still deliver positioning, navigation and timing service. Four are needed for a fix. His wording was careful. NavIC cannot provide standalone positioning, he said, but its timing service is functional. The distinction is real. Positioning needs a fourth satellite to solve for the error inside the receiver's own clock. Timing is a lighter demand. The difficulty is the sentence after it. Users face no operational vulnerability, the reply said, because Indian receivers work in a multi-constellation environment combining NavIC with GPS, Galileo and GLONASS. The armed forces do the same. One arm of the government defends the condition of NavIC by pointing at GPS. Another arm, four weeks later, writes GPS out of the authorised list for the sectors where failure hurts most. The rest of the picture is thin. IRNSS-1B went up in 2014 and has outlived its ten-year design life. NVS-02 was stranded in transfer orbit in January 2025 after a valve failure. NVS-03 sits ready at Sriharikota with a launch expected in early September, and two more are to follow without a date. Why a clock is a target Between November 2023 and February 2025, airlines reported 465 GPS interference and spoofing incidents in Indian airspace, a figure the Civil Aviation Ministry has confirmed in Parliament. Most were in the Amritsar and Jammu corridors. Readers here will not need that geography explained. The problem has since moved inland. Spoofing was reported around Indira Gandhi International Airport late last year, with interference logged at Kolkata, Mumbai, Chennai and Bengaluru. The DGCA now wants pilots and controllers to report a GNSS anomaly within ten minutes. Timing sits underneath much more than aviation. Mobile networks hand a call from one tower to the next on the assumption that both agree about the microsecond. Power grids compare phase measurements across state boundaries. Every log a forensic investigation depends on is a claim about when something happened. That is why time is worth attacking. An adversary who shifts your clock steals nothing. He corrupts the record that any later inquiry will read. Which is also the strongest argument for the new rules. GPS is a foreign military signal, it was withheld from India once, and it is being interfered with along the western border now. Two routes to the same room The objection is not to the direction. It is to the order of operations. Rule 8(2) obliges the Director, Legal Metrology to publish the addresses and access protocols of every authorised timing service. No such list is public. Engineers were asking for exactly this in 2022, when CERT-In first told organisations to synchronise their clocks with NIC or NPL servers. Publication is now a legal duty and still has not happened. Capacity is no clearer. Answering an RTI filed by MediaNama in December 2022, CSIR-NPL said it ran 20 NTP servers, all of them at one location in Delhi. NIC declined to give a count, citing security. Those figures are nearly four years old, and nothing public has replaced them. Then there is the part that is easy to miss. NavIC does not keep independent time. Published metrology work on the IRNSS Network Timing Facility describes its time scales as linked to UTC(NPLI), the realisation of universal time maintained at CSIR-NPL in Delhi. For a bank in Jammu, NavIC and the national time servers are not two independent sources of truth. They are two routes to the same laboratory. The rules also decline to say how accurate is accurate enough. Rule 2(a) defines accuracy as conformity to IST without a millisecond or microsecond figure anywhere in eight pages, and Rule 10 provides for audits against a standard the text never states. Rule 11 says a breach is punishable under the Act without naming a section or an amount, and Rule 8(5) lets the Director charge a fee for legally mandated time. Bottom Line Sovereign time is the right objective. A country that refused a navigation signal during a war should not run its banks and its grid on a foreign military system it cannot audit or repair. But a mandate is not a capability, and withdrawing the fallback before the primary is ready produces exposure with better paperwork. Three things ought to be public before these rules bite. The authorised source list Rule 8(2) already requires. The current number and physical distribution of NTP and PTP servers at NPL and NIC. And an answer to a question nobody in government has yet been asked: what happens to Indian time if the Delhi facility goes dark? (The author studies Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence at Rutgers University, New Jersey, USA. stories.headline: GST, auto, UPI data signal August growth
stories.title: GST, auto, UPI data signal August growth
stories.summary: New Delhi: Several macro indicators released on Tuesday brought further economic cheer, underscoring domestic resilience in the face of tariff headwinds and the lingering crisis in West Asia. India's total goods and services tax (GST) collections rose 14.8% from a year earlier to Rs 2 lakh crore in August, while bulk car sales surged 36% to 448,000, putting India on course to hit 5 million units in the current fiscal year.The Unified Payments Interface (UPI) platform processed a record 24.51 billion transactions worth Rs 29.82 lakh crore in the month, underlining consumer demand. Year-on-year, transaction volume increased 22%, while transaction value went up 20%. Power consumption rose 12.9% YoY to 169 billion units.Also Read: India seeks applications for remaining raw sugar import quotaHealthy ConsumptionThese numbers signal momentum persisting in July-September after data released on Monday showed the economy expanded by a better-than-expected 7.8% in April-June.133691042Petrol sales rose 7.9% and diesel sales 6.5% year-on-year in August, aided by increased mobility, stronger vehicle sales and an expanding economy. Aviation turbine fuel (ATF) sales rose 1.4%, while cooking gas sales fell 16.1%, according to preliminary data from the oil ministry.GST collections from imports continued to be the primary performance driver, accelerating 29% from a year earlier to Rs 62,604 crore, while domestic revenue from the levy rose 9.3% to more than Rs 1.37 lakh crore in August, buoyed by durable demand at home.The strong GST growth, combined with 7.8% GDP expansion in the June quarter, reflected the strength of the Indian economy despite geopolitical conflicts and global economic uncertainty, said Abhishek Jain, partner and national head, indirect tax at KPMG in India.Also Read: Indian banks slash FCNR deposit rates by up to 310 basis pointsThe latest numbers portray a mix of healthy consumption, expanding formalisation of the economy and improving compliance."These collections are a very reliable barometer of the economy since they cover both goods and services across the country," said MS Mani, partner, tax at Deloitte India. "There does not appear to be any slowdown in economic activity and consumption in India, despite the tariff headwinds and west Asia situation."Experts are optimistic that, despite an uncertain global outlook, GST collections will continue to surge from October onwards, backed by upcoming festivals when demand for consumer goods traditionally grows. "With the festive season round the corner, revenue collections over the next couple of months are likely to trend higher, supported by increased consumer spending," said Saurabh Agarwal, tax partner at EY India.Agarwal said the concurrent rise in imports showed the need for deeper localisation and import substitution.After refunds, net GST collections stood at Rs 1.68 lakh crore, up 8.3% year-on-year. Refunds surged 68% to Rs 31,795 crore, tempering the growth in the net tax take but also reflecting a sharp rise in refund processing.Mani said the sustained strength in collections should prompt the GST Council to look at easing input tax credit restrictions, rationalising audits and reducing compliance requirements, when it meets next on September 12."Businesses would expect fewer restrictions on ITC (input tax credit), centralisation of audits across states, simpler compliance for service providers, improved ease of registration and deregistration," said Mani.Total gross GST revenue during April to August rose 11% from a year earlier at Rs 10,42,757 crore. Total net GST revenue during the period increased 9% at Rs 8,89,523 crore.

opening: Srinagar, Sep 01: The Jammu and Kashmir Government on Tuesday ordered a major administrative reshuffle, transferring and posting 136 officers of the Jammu and Kashmir Administrative Service (JKAS) across various departments, institutions and districts.
The transfers were ordered with immediate effect by the General Administration Department (GAD) through Government Order No. 1463-JK(GAD) of 2026, dated September 1.

stories.title: The politics of an endless tomorrow
stories.summary: Politics has a curious relationship with unfinished promises. A promise that is fulfilled ceases to be a promise; it becomes a fact. A promise that fails, however, can acquire an unexpected political afterlife. It can be repeated, refined, mourned, blamed on circumstances, and eventually presented to the electorate once again—as though its previous failure were itself evidence of the sincerity of those who made it. In this peculiar economy of democratic politics, the unfulfilled promise can become more durable than the fulfilled one. The unfolding political episode involving Aga Ruhullah Mehdi appears to be approaching precisely such a moment. Mehdi is expected to resign from the National Conference and from the Lok Sabha in November, following his increasingly public disagreement with the party over its approach to Article 370. If the resignation is followed by a by-election, he is likely to return to the electorate seeking a fresh mandate. There is, of course, nothing inherently illegitimate about any of this. A politician may leave a party when he believes that it has abandoned a principle, and a citizen has every right to seek electoral vindication. But the circumstances raise a question that is considerably more important than the resignation itself: what exactly is the electorate being asked to renew? Mehdi was elected to Parliament in 2024 in a political campaign in which the restoration of Article 370 occupied a central place. He did not present the issue merely as a matter of historical sentiment. He spoke of carrying the political aspirations of Jammu and Kashmir to Parliament and of pursuing the struggle for constitutional rights. After entering Parliament, he continued to raise Article 370 and criticised the National Conference for what he regarded as its retreat from the position on which it had sought the people’s mandate. He has also spoken of a political roadmap in which restoration of Article 370 would constitute an important step towards the larger objective of autonomy. That is precisely why the present moment demands more than another declaration of commitment. Where is the roadmap? The question may sound almost offensively mundane in the presence of such a grand constitutional aspiration. But democracy is often saved from political theatre by mundane questions. What is the strategy? What are its institutional mechanisms? Who are its political allies? What constitutional route is envisaged? What parliamentary arithmetic is being pursued? What political constituencies outside Jammu and Kashmir are being cultivated? What are the stages of the campaign? What constitutes measurable progress? And after two years, how far has that strategy actually travelled? These are not questions designed to diminish Article 370. They are questions designed to take the promise seriously. There is a fundamental difference between saying that Article 370 ought to be restored and telling an electorate that one will fight to restore it. The former is a political conviction. The latter is a claim of political agency. Once agency is claimed, accountability follows almost automatically. The problem, therefore, is not that Mehdi continues to believe in the restoration of Article 370. He is perfectly entitled to that belief. Nor is the problem that he considers the National Conference insufficiently committed to it. He is entitled to leave the party if that is his considered judgment. The difficulty arises when an extraordinarily complicated constitutional objective is repeatedly presented to the electorate without a sufficiently credible account of the route by which it is supposed to be achieved. A constitutional aspiration is not a strategy. A speech is not a strategy. A protest is not a strategy. And, with due respect to the theatre of political resignation, a resignation is certainly not a strategy. This distinction becomes particularly important because restoration of Article 370 is not a conventional policy demand. The constitutional architecture of Jammu and Kashmir has changed profoundly since August 2019. The Supreme Court has also adjudicated upon the constitutional changes. The present institutional arrangement is therefore not something that can simply be rewound by political will. Anyone seeking its reversal must confront a formidable constitutional and political reality. That does not make restoration impossible in the metaphysical sense. Constitutional orders are made by politics and can, in principle, be altered by politics. But the greater the institutional distance between a political aspiration and its realisation, the greater the obligation upon the politician to explain the bridge between the two. This is where Mehdi’s political argument deserves to be tested rather than merely applauded or condemned. If the National Conference had a “proper roadmap,” as Mehdi himself suggested in 2024, what happened to it? If restoration of Article 370 was to be the first step towards autonomy, what were the subsequent steps? If the strategy depended upon building a broader national political coalition, where is that coalition? If parliamentary pressure was central to the strategy, what measurable political pressure has been generated? If the answer is that the political environment made progress impossible, then the next question is unavoidable: what precisely was the strategy designed to overcome that environment? It is not enough to say that the objective is difficult. Politics is, almost by definition, the art of pursuing objectives under conditions in which they are difficult. The BJP’s presence at the Centre was not a secret in 2024. The constitutional consequences of 2019 were not unknown. The political obstacles to restoring Article 370 were not suddenly discovered after the election. They were part of the very circumstances in which the mandate was sought. The electorate was therefore not merely asked to endorse a grievance. It was asked to endorse a politician who claimed that the grievance could be politically pursued. Two years later, the burden is to explain what that pursuit has yielded. And here the proposed by-election produces an irony that should not be lost on anyone interested in democratic accountability. Imagine the electorate being approached once again with essentially the same proposition. The candidate says: Give me your vote. I will fight for Article 370. The voter may reasonably respond: You already had our vote. The candidate may then say: Yes, but the party did not fight. The voter can ask: Then what did you do? The candidate may answer: I have now left the party. And the voter may quite reasonably ask the question that political rhetoric would prefer to postpone: Why should leaving the party entitle you to another mandate when the first mandate has not yet been accounted for? This is not an argument that Mehdi had the power to restore Article 370. He did not. To demand such an outcome from an individual MP would be both politically naïve and constitutionally unserious. The relevant standard is not whether he achieved the impossible. The standard is whether he can demonstrate a coherent political strategy proportionate to the promise on which he sought office. There is an important distinction between failure and non-performance. A politician may pursue a credible strategy and fail because circumstances overwhelm him. That is an ordinary feature of politics. But if there is no discernible strategy, then failure becomes almost impossible to distinguish from political inertia. And when political inertia is wrapped in increasingly emphatic rhetoric, the electorate has a right to become suspicious. This is where the promise of Article 370 risks becoming something more than a constitutional demand. It can become a form of political capital whose value depends precisely upon its remaining unresolved. An unresolved cause is remarkably convenient politically. It cannot be disproved by events because its fulfilment is always deferred. It allows the politician to say that the struggle continues, that the circumstances were unfavourable, that others betrayed the cause, and that another mandate is therefore necessary. The political calendar moves forward. The promise does not. The electorate is asked to move with it. This is the danger of perpetual political promise. It transforms the absence of an outcome into an argument for another opportunity. The politician does not necessarily have to demonstrate that the strategy worked; he only has to demonstrate that the cause remains emotionally alive. For a society with Kashmir’s political history, this is particularly consequential. Constitutional questions here are not abstract matters of institutional design. They are intertwined with memory, identity, dignity, loss and competing understandings of political belonging. The language surrounding Article 370 therefore possesses a moral intensity that ordinary electoral promises rarely acquire. For that reason, politicians who invoke it should be subject to greater intellectual scrutiny, not less. There is something almost paradoxical in demanding that citizens vote again for the restoration of something that has not moved appreciably closer to restoration during the first mandate. Yet perhaps this is the point at which democratic politics must resist its own sentimental tendencies. Conviction is not competence. Persistence is not progress. And repetition is not evidence. Mehdi has been vocal. He has spoken in Parliament. He has criticised his party. He has continued to foreground Article 370. None of this should be denied. But the question is not whether he has been politically active. The question is whether that activity constitutes a strategy capable of producing political consequences. If he believes the National Conference constrained him, he should explain the precise nature of those constraints. If he believes independence will make the struggle more effective, he should explain why. If he believes a fresh mandate will strengthen his hand, he should explain what the new mandate will enable him to do that the previous one did not. Otherwise, the by-election risks becoming a curious democratic ritual in which the electorate is invited to vote twice on the same promise without being given an account of what happened between the two votes. That would be an inversion of the logic of representation. An election is not merely a mechanism for expressing hope. It is also a mechanism for remembering. The voter carries the previous mandate into the next election. Political time is cumulative. The second vote cannot simply erase the first. The politician who asks for renewal must confront the record that makes renewal necessary. This is why the impending contest, if it occurs, should not be reduced to a personal battle between Mehdi and the National Conference. It should be treated as a question about the meaning of political accountability itself. The National Conference certainly owes the people an explanation for the gap between its promises and its present conduct. If it promised to fight for Article 370, it must explain what “fight” meant and why its political conduct subsequently departed from that commitment. But Mehdi owes the electorate something as well. He must explain what his fight produced. Not what he believes. Not what he said. Not what he intended. What did it produce? That is a harder standard, but it is also a democratic one. There is perhaps an even more uncomfortable question. If restoration of Article 370 is neither presently achievable through any identifiable political route nor supported by a credible strategy capable of altering the existing constitutional order, then is it responsible to continue presenting its restoration as though it were an imminent electoral deliverable? A politician may say that a cause will take decades. That is legitimate. But then he should say so. He should tell the electorate that he is asking not for a mandate to deliver an outcome within a foreseeable political horizon, but for a mandate to participate in a long historical struggle whose result may lie beyond the tenure of any individual politician. There would be intellectual honesty in such an admission. What is problematic is to oscillate between the language of immediate political mandate and the temporal reality of an indefinite constitutional struggle. The people deserve to know which of the two they are being offered. Mehdi may ultimately decide that the National Conference has failed him. He may conclude that leaving the party is necessary to preserve his political integrity. He may contest a by-election and place himself once again before the people. All of that is legitimate. But legitimacy cuts both ways. The candidate has the right to ask for another vote. The voter has the right to ask for an account. And perhaps the most important question in the next election will therefore not be whether the people still believe in Article 370. They may very well continue to believe in it. The question will be whether they believe that Ruhullah Mehdi has demonstrated a credible political capacity to advance it. He cannot reasonably ask the electorate to treat 2026 as though 2024 never happened. The first mandate exists. Its promises exist. Its limitations exist. Its record exists. Before another promise is made, there must be a reckoning with the old one. Otherwise, the political bargain becomes remarkably simple: make the promise, receive the mandate, explain the failure, resign, return, and make the promise again. The electorate deserves a more demanding conception of politics. Article 370 may remain a legitimate political aspiration. But if it is to be presented as an electoral programme, then it must confront the elementary disciplines of political reasoning: What is the route? What is the strategy? What has been attempted? What has been achieved? What has failed? And why should the next mandate produce a different result? Until those questions are answered, the problem is not merely that the promise remains unfinished. The problem is that the promise itself has never been made to account for reality. Dr Zahid Sultan, Independent Researcher Based in Srinagar, India.

stories.summary: Srinagar, Sep 1: Kashmir's head priest Mirwaiz Umar Farooq on Tuesday warned that growing human intervention in Jammu and Kashmir’s fragile ecosystems was pushing the region towards an ecological crisis, urging both the government and people to shoulder responsibility for protecting the environment. Expressing concern over the condition of Dal Lake and Wular Lake, Mirwaiz said that while development of tourism and creation of facilities for visitors were important, such initiatives could not come at the cost of environmental balance. “Dal Lake and Wular Lake are facing serious ecological pressure. We all want to develop tourism and create facilities for visitors, but we cannot afford development at the cost of environmental balance,” he told reporters here. He said unplanned construction in mountainous areas and tourist destinations, coupled with roads being constructed without adequate regard for the terrain and environment, was placing additional pressure on the region’s fragile ecological systems. “This is an ecological and environmental disaster, and we must act before it is too late,” Mirwaiz said. Referring specifically to Pahalgam, he expressed concern over what he described as large-scale construction and the haphazard manner in which roads were being built in the area. Mirwaiz said the government must certainly be held accountable for ensuring sustainable planning and enforcing environmental regulations, but citizens could not absolve themselves of their own responsibilities. “While the government can be held accountable, we cannot ignore our responsibilities. It is high time that we shoulder our responsibility to prevent natural disasters,” he said. He said the increasing frequency of extreme weather-related events in Kashmir—including hailstorms, cloudbursts and flash floods—was deeply disturbing and should prompt serious introspection about the relationship between human activity and nature. “The trend in Kashmir, like rising incidents of hailstorms, cloudbursts and flash floods, is disturbing and signals human intervention with nature,” Mirwaiz said. He called for a balance between development and conservation, saying tourism infrastructure should be planned in a manner that protects the region’s mountains, forests, water bodies and other fragile ecosystems. Mirwaiz's remarks come amid growing concern over the vulnerability of Jammu and Kashmir's mountainous landscape to extreme weather events and the environmental consequences of unplanned development.
